title: Moore's law
description: Observation on the growth of integrated circuit capacity
wiki_lead:
Moore's law is the observation that the number of transistors in an integrated circuit (IC) doubles about every two years, with minimal increase in cost. Despite the name, Moore's law describes an empirical relationship, not a scientific law. This type of observation, an experience curve effect, quantifies efficiency gains from learned experience in production.
The observation is named after Gordon Moore, the co-founder of Fairchild Semiconductor and Intel and former Chief Executive Officer of the latter, who in 1965 noted that the number of components per integrated circuit had been doubling every year, and projected that this rate of growth would continue for at least another decade. In 1975, looking forward to the next decade, he revised the forecast to doubling every two years, a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 41%. Moore's empirical evidence did not imply that the historical trend would continue; nevertheless, his prediction has held since 1975 and has since become known as a law.
Moore's prediction has been used in the semiconductor industry to guide long-term planning and to set targets for research and development (R&D). Advancements in digital electronics, such as the reduction in quality-adjusted prices of microprocessors, the increase in memory capacity (RAM and flash), the improvement of sensors, and even the number and size of pixels in digital cameras, are strongly linked to Moore's law. These ongoing changes in digital electronics have been a driving force of technological and social change, productivity, and economic growth.
Industry experts have not reached a consensus on exactly when Moore's law will cease to apply. Microprocessor architects report that semiconductor advancement has slowed industry-wide since around 2010, slightly below the pace predicted by Moore's law. In September 2022, Nvidia's then-CEO Jensen Huang considered Moore's law dead, while Intel's then-CEO Pat Gelsinger had the opposite view.

History
In 1959, Douglas Engelbart studied the projected downscaling of integrated circuit (IC) size, publishing his results in the article "Microelectronics, and the Art of Similitude". Engelbart presented his findings at the 1960 International Solid-State Circuits Conference, where Moore was present in the audience.
In 1965, Gordon Moore, who at the time was working as the director of research and development at Fairchild Semiconductor, was asked to contribute to the thirty-fifth-anniversary issue of Electronics magazine with a prediction on the future of the semiconductor components industry over the next ten years. His response was a brief article entitled "Cramming more components onto integrated circuits". Within his editorial, he speculated that by 1975 it would be possible to contain as many as 65000 components on a single quarter-square-inch (~ 1.6 cm2) semiconductor.

grok_lead: Moore's law is the observation made by Gordon E. Moore, co-founder of Intel Corporation, in a 1965 article published in Electronics magazine, predicting that the number of components (such as transistors) on an integrated circuit would double every year, thereby enabling exponential growth in computing capability at decreasing costs. In 1975, Moore revised this forecast to a doubling approximately every two years, based on updated data from semiconductor advancements, a rate that became the standard interpretation of the law. The term " Moore's law " itself was popularized around 1970 by California Institute of Technology professor Carver Mead, who used it to describe the trend during discussions on very-large-scale integration (VLSI) design. This empirical rule has profoundly shaped the semiconductor industry since its inception, serving as a self-fulfilling prophecy that guided research, investment, and manufacturing innovations for decades. From the mid-1960s onward, the law correlated with dramatic increases in transistor densityâfrom about 60 components per chip in 1965 to hundreds of billions by the mid-2020sâwhile keeping production costs relatively stable or declining, which fueled the miniaturization and affordability of electronic devices. Key enablers included advances in photolithography, materials science, and fabrication processes, allowing companies like Intel to pack more functionality into smaller spaces without proportional cost hikes. Beyond hardware, Moore's law has had cascading effects on the broader computing ecosystem, driving the proliferation of personal computers, smartphones, the internet, and artificial intelligence by exponentially enhancing processing power and energy efficiency. For instance, the law underpinned the transition from mainframes to ubiquitous mobile computing, with transistor counts aligning closely to the predicted trajectory until physical limits began challenging traditional scaling in the late 2010s and 2020s. Although debates persist on its ongoing validity amid atomic-scale constraintsâas of 2025, the doubling pace has slowedâthe principle continues to inspire alternative paradigms like 3D integration and quantum computing to sustain progress.
